facts.content: Patient reports an intensely itchy, red rash for 4 days.
facts.source_text: CC: intensely itchy, red rash x 4 d

facts.content: The rash has been present for 4 days.
facts.source_text: CC: intensely itchy, red rash x 4 d

facts.content: The rash is distributed on the chest, hands, and antecubital fossae.
The rash interferes with the patient’s sleep and work.
The patient reports that the skin is sore and cracked without bleeding or pus.
facts.source_text: Skin sore, cracked; no bleed, pus

facts.content: The patient denies fever, cough, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms.
facts.source_text: Denies fever, cough, SOB, GI/GU sx

facts.content: The patient tried over-the-counter steroid cream and antihistamines with minimal relief.
facts.source_text: Tried OTC steroid cream & antihistamines → minimal relief

facts.content: Patient has a history of eczema previously limited to the arms.
Patient has a history of childhood asthma that has resolved.
Patient takes no routine medications.
No allergies are reported.
Patient lives with flatmates.
Patient works as a pharmacy project manager.
Patient is a non-smoker.
Patient drinks a few beers per week.
Patient hikes but this activity is limited by the rash.
Tele-exam shows erythematous, dry, eczematous patches on the chest, hands, and antecubital areas.
facts.source_text: Tele-exam: erythematous, dry, eczematous patches chest/hands/antecubital

facts.content: No discharge or bleeding is noted from the skin lesions on tele-exam.
Assessment is an acute eczema flare with severe pruritus.
facts.source_text: Acute eczema flare w/ severe pruritus

facts.content: Prescribe a higher-potency topical corticosteroid.
Prescribe an emollient wash and moisturizer to be used twice daily and after showers.
facts.source_text: Rx emollient wash/moisturizer; use bid & after showers

facts.content: Prescribe fexofenadine for itch.
Counsel the patient to avoid irritants.
Advise the patient to keep a trigger diary including soaps, fabrics, and other possible triggers.
Follow up in 7 to 10 days or sooner if symptoms worsen.
facts.source_text: F/U in 7–10 d or sooner if worsening
